A 58-year-old male presents to the emergency department with cramping abdominal pain and yellow
discoloration of the skin. The pain began last night and is accompanied by nausea and non-bloody
vomiting. He has no significant medical history. His vital signs include a temperature of 39 ºC (102.2
ºF), pulse of 117/min, blood pressure of 151/69 mmHg, respiratory rate of 14/min, and SpO2 of 100%
on room air. On examination, the patient appears ill with jaundice and scleral icterus. There is
moderate tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory results reveal leukocytosis and
hyperbilirubinemia. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Answer Choices: (A)
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) (B) Administration of IV antibiotics with
ceftriaxone (C) Observation with supportive care (D) Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy (E)
Gastroenterology consult for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (F) Repeat liver
function tests after 24 hours (G) Emergent general surgery consult (H) Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid
(HIDA) scan (I) Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (J) CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV
contrast
 A. Repeat liver function tests after 24 hours
B. Observation with supportive care
C. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
D. Gastroenterology consult for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
E. Administration of IV antibiotics with ceftriaxone
F. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
G. Emergent general surgery consult
H. Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy
I. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography

J. Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan
